---
title: "1. Mapping crt K76T in the Greater Horn of Africa"
description: >
  From a STAVE data object to maps, country trends and probability
  statements: the chloroquine-resistance marker crt K76T across the eight
  IGAD countries, 1989-2024.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
```

The *Plasmodium falciparum* crt K76T mutation is the main marker of
chloroquine resistance. Chloroquine was replaced as the first-line treatment
for falciparum malaria across East Africa between the late 1990s and the
mid-2000s, and where it stopped being used the resistant parasites lost
their advantage. This tutorial maps K76T across the eight member states of
IGAD (Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan and
Uganda) from 1989 to 2024, and asks:

- how prevalence changed in each country, with honest uncertainty;
- where the chloroquine-sensitive parasite is now dominant;
- where the data are too thin to say.

It takes the data from a STAVE object, the format of the public collation of
antimalarial drug-resistance surveys. The same data ship with the package as
`igad_crt76t`, for readers without STAVE.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data: a STAVE object

STAVE stores studies, surveys and variant counts. The public data set is an
R object of a little over 250 kB; reading it needs the
[STAVE package](https://github.com/mrc-ide/STAVE).

```{r stave}
url <- paste0("https://github.com/IDEELResearch/scrub/raw/2d85d021efe1c93dc55300610d944c9fbaf4af1a/",
              "analysis/data-out/stave_data_2026.03.17.rds")
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
download.file(url, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
stave <- suppressWarnings(readRDS(tmp))
stave
```

To get the prevalence of one variant, use `get_prevalence()`. It counts
every survey that genotyped the codon, whatever the format the study used
(single loci, multi-locus haplotypes), and for a mutant includes the surveys
where it was absent. Reading the raw counts with `get_counts()` for the
exact string `"crt:76:T"` would miss some of these surveys, and for a rare
mutant almost all of the zeros (see [tutorial 2](k13-622i.html)).

```{r prevalence}
igad <- c("Djibouti", "Eritrea", "Ethiopia", "Kenya", "Somalia", "South Sudan", "Sudan", "Uganda")
p <- stave$get_prevalence("crt:76:T")
p <- p[p$country_name %in% igad & p$denominator > 0, ]
nrow(p)
table(p$country_name)
```

The strict Horn of Africa (Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia) has only 13
surveys, and Somalia none: too few for a space-time model. With the other
IGAD members there are 272 surveys from 90 studies. These are exactly the
surveys in `igad_crt76t`:

```{r same-as-packaged}
all.equal(sort(p$survey_id), sort(igad_crt76t$survey_id))
surveys <- igad_crt76t
```

Each survey has a location, counts, and a date, `collection_day`: the
middle of the collection window, or the date the study gave. Most windows
are a few months, some surveys give only a date (no window), and some
studies report only a span of years:

```{r windows}
window_years <- as.numeric(surveys$collection_end - surveys$collection_start) / 365.25
summary(window_years)
sum(window_years > 2, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The `r sum(window_years > 2, na.rm = TRUE)` surveys spanning more than two
years are placed at the middle of their window. Section 7 checks whether
that matters.

## 2. The spatial frame

The package ships the first-level administrative units of the eight
countries, from geoBoundaries (Uganda by district; see `?igad_adm1`). The
national boundary files come from different sources, so neighbouring units
across a border do not quite touch: `adjacency_snap = 2000` makes units
whose borders come within 2 km neighbours. Islands are linked to the nearest
unit of their own country.

```{r frame}
fr <- areal_frame(igad_adm1, id = "id", groups = c(country = "country"),
                  link_within = "country", adjacency_snap = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
fr
```

```{r frame-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot(fr)
```

Building the frame computes the eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian, a
one-off step (here a second; a minute or so for several thousand units).
In a real analysis, build it once and save it with `saveRDS()`.

## 3. Time, and the survey data

Yearly steps from 1989 to 2024:

```{r time}
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "year")
tf
```

`areal_data()` puts each survey in an area (point in polygon, snapping
points just outside every polygon, such as coastal sites, to the nearest
unit) and a year, and pools surveys in the same area and year:

```{r data}
d <- areal_data(surveys, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day")
d
```

```{r data-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(d)
```

The data are clumped: Kenya and Uganda are well surveyed, Somalia not at
all, and 199 of the 9,648 area-years have data. The model fills the gaps
from neighbouring areas and years; how confidently it can do so is part of
the answer.

## 4. Fitting

A first run with the defaults (four chains of 3,000 iterations, in parallel)
takes under a minute here:

```{r pilot, eval = FALSE}
pilot <- fit_areal(d)
diagnose(pilot)
```

```{r load, include = FALSE}
cache <- readRDS("_cache/crt76t.rds")
fit <- cache$fit
fit$data$frame <- fr              # the cache stores fits without their frame
fit_short <- cache$fit_short
fit_short$data$frame <- fr
```

```{r pilot-checks, echo = FALSE}
cache$pilot_checks
```

`diagnose()` checks the R-hat and effective sample size (ESS) of every
parameter, including the latent prevalence of every observed cell. Here the
pilot already passes, which is not guaranteed: sparse or mostly-zero data
mix more slowly (see [tutorial 2](k13-622i.html)). Results for publication
deserve a longer run anyway, with more draws for the tails of the
intervals and for exceedance probabilities:

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(d, control = list(n_iter = 20000, n_burn = 5000, n_store = 250, theta_thin = 10),
                 checkpoint_dir = "chains/crt76t")
```

It takes `r round(cache$built$seconds[["fit"]] / 60)` minutes per chain,
with the chains in parallel. With `checkpoint_dir` set, an interrupted run
picks up where it stopped when the same call is run again.

```{r diagnose}
cache$checks
```

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

```{r traces, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

How to read the hyperparameters:

- `sigma` sets the size of the variation around the trend on the logit
  scale.
- `rho_s` close to 1 means neighbouring units are strongly alike.
- `rho_t` close to 1 means prevalence changes slowly from year to year.
- `sigma_n` is the scatter between surveys in the same area and year,
  beyond what the field explains (different sites, sampling, methods).

The `trend` coefficient is half the change in logit prevalence over the
window, before the field: a strongly negative value is the regional
decline.

## 5. Predicting the full surface

`predict()` reconstructs the prevalence of every unit in every year, once
per posterior draw, and aggregates each draw to the countries. Country
estimates here are unweighted means over their units; with population or
parasite-burden data, give them as `weights`.

```{r predict}
pr <- predict(fit, groups = "country", exceedance = c(0.1, 0.5), verbose = FALSE)
pr
head(pr$area[, c("id", "country", "time", "y", "k", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")])
```

Maps for three years, made from `sf::st_as_sf()`, which joins a year's
estimates to the polygons:

```{r maps, fig.height = 4}
years <- c("2000", "2010", "2024")
m <- do.call(rbind, lapply(years, function(y) sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = y)))
ggplot(m) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mean), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("K76T\nprevalence", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_void()
```

Country trends, with the 95% interval and the surveys (pooled by unit and
year; point size shows the number tested):

```{r countries, fig.height = 6}
plot(pr, group = "country", ids = c("Kenya", "Uganda", "Sudan", "Ethiopia", "South Sudan", "Eritrea"))
```

```{r country-table}
subset(pr$groups$country, time %in% c("2000", "2024"),
       select = c(id, time, mean, q2.5, q97.5))
```

## 6. Probability statements, and where the data run out

The posterior answers questions directly. Where is the
chloroquine-sensitive parasite now dominant, that is, where is K76T
prevalence probably below 10%?

```{r prob-low, fig.height = 4.5}
m24 <- sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = "2024")
m24$p_below_10 <- 1 - m24$p_gt_0.1
ggplot(m24) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = p_below_10), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("P(prevalence\n< 10%), 2024", limits = c(0, 1), option = "magma") +
  theme_void()
```

The units where that probability is above 0.9, by country:

```{r prob-low-table}
table(m24$country[m24$p_below_10 > 0.9])
```

Nearly all are in Kenya and Uganda, which have most of the surveys, and
most of the recent ones. Elsewhere the probability is moderate. The decline
may well have happened there too, but the data cannot show it.

Uncertainty is not uniform. The posterior standard deviation in 2024, beside
the total number tested in each unit over the whole period:

```{r uncertainty, fig.height = 4}
m24$tested <- tapply(pr$area$k, pr$area$id, sum)[m24$id]
m24$tested[m24$tested == 0] <- NA
g1 <- ggplot(m24) + geom_sf(aes(fill = sd), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("posterior sd,\n2024") + theme_void()
g2 <- ggplot(m24) + geom_sf(aes(fill = tested), colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("tested,\n1989-2024", trans = "log10", na.value = "grey95") + theme_void()
patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2)
```

The median standard deviation by country:

```{r sd-by-country}
round(tapply(m24$sd, m24$country, median), 2)
```

Where there are few or no surveys nearby, as in Djibouti, Eritrea, Somalia
and much of Sudan, the estimate leans on the regional trend and the
intervals widen. A map of the posterior mean alone would hide this.

## 7. Sensitivity: surveys with long collection windows

`r cache$n_long` surveys span more than two years. Refitting without them
(the precomputing script does both) shows whether placing them at the
middle of their window drives the trends:

```{r sensitivity, fig.height = 4}
pr_short <- predict(fit_short, groups = "country", verbose = FALSE)
cols <- c("id", "time", "date", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")
both <- rbind(cbind(pr$groups$country[cols], data = "all surveys"),
              cbind(pr_short$groups$country[cols], data = "windows <= 2 years"))
both <- both[both$id %in% c("Kenya", "Uganda", "Sudan", "South Sudan"), ]
ggplot(both, aes(date, mean, colour = data, fill = data)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "K76T prevalence", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r sensitivity-diff}
diff <- merge(pr$groups$country, pr_short$groups$country, by = c("id", "time"))
diff$change <- diff$mean.y - diff$mean.x
head(diff[order(-abs(diff$change)), c("id", "time", "mean.x", "mean.y", "change")], 4)
```

The trends in Kenya and Uganda, where the data are dense, barely move. The
largest changes, about `r round(max(abs(diff$change)), 2)` on the prevalence
scale, are in Sudan and South Sudan around 2012-2013, inside the intervals
of either fit. The share of long-window surveys is not what matters: Uganda has the
largest, 16 of its 79, and barely moves. What matters is how sparse the
other data are. In Sudan and South Sudan, each survey carries more weight.

## 8. Taking the results away

The tables are ordinary data frames, and the maps ordinary `sf` objects:

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(pr$area, "crt76t_by_unit_year.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pr$groups$country, "crt76t_by_country_year.csv", row.names = FALSE)
sf::st_write(sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = "2024"), "crt76t_2024.gpkg")
```

The posterior draws of the parameters and of every observed cell are
available for your own summaries with `posterior::as_draws_df(fit)`.
